noi_dung:
Cultivators Must Bear Suffering

There is a saying: "Bear suffering and suffering ends; enjoy blessings and blessings dissolve." Why must we in cultivating the Way practice asceticism? Each day we eat but one meal because we wish to end suffering. Suffering ended—there will be joy.

As for blessings, some should be enjoyed and some not. Blessings to enjoy are those our own hands have made—like a fine house, fine clothes, fine food, a fine car. Yet remember: once those are enjoyed out, blessings dissolve too—and in the blessings-bank ledger, the balance stands empty.

Blessings not to be enjoyed are those not of our own making. They come to us by tricks—like money stolen from others. Spending such gains unlawfully, the law will surely punish. Thus you have overdrawn—running a deficit in the blessings-bank ledger.

Enjoying blessings, once enjoyed out, blessings are gone—let alone deliberately enjoying blessings not to be enjoyed. Then not only are blessings spent, you go bankrupt besides. Hence blessings must never be enjoyed out—enjoyed out, blessings end; suffering may be borne out—borne out, suffering ends. As people, remember this. Meeting hardship and adversity, gladly accept adversity. Then no resentment—you harbor no discontent.

One who has studied the Buddhadharma thinks and acts unlike worldly people. One way follows birth-and-death's current, creating karma; the cultivator goes against birth-and-death's current, dissolving karma. In every circumstance, such people keep the mind at peace, feeling no suffering. There is a saying: "Only tasting the utmost suffering can one become supreme." Truly a maxim of truth.

Now I tell a gongan for your reference. The last emperor of the Ming was the Chongzhen Emperor. As a sovereign, he had wisdom enough, but lacked the blessings for the throne. Why? Because meeting suffering, he never bore it out to the end. In a past life he was a novice, dying before receiving the Complete Precepts—so he remained a little novice. As a novice, he took on all heavy chores—hauling water, chopping wood. He bore it, swallowing resentment, toiling daily to guard the Way-place. One day, climbing the roof to mend it, he slipped and fell to his death. Fellow cultivators hurried to tell the Abbot. The Abbot, knowing this little novice's karma, sought to help his disciple bear suffering out—and before the assembly declared: "This little novice worked carelessly, slipped and died, harming the Way-place. He has committed the offense of damaging the permanent dwelling—deserving punishment. Tie his corpse to a team of horses and drag it till it falls apart. No coffin burial needed." The fellow cultivators, hearing the Abbot, could not bear it—moved by fellow-cultivator friendship to pity. Disobeying the Abbot's order, they conferred: "We are Dharma brothers, cultivating in one Way-place—how let him be horse-dragged? We must bury him properly." Agreed, they pooled money for a coffin and buried him in the mountains.

Through bitter toil serving the monastery, the little novice had gathered merit—and so was reborn as emperor—the Chongzhen Emperor. But he reigned only sixteen years, meeting a world in great turmoil—within, Li Zicheng rebelling; without, the Qing invading. Through those years, never a single peaceful day—unceasing pressure and worry. Precisely his Dharma brothers' kindness harmed him—not letting him bear suffering out. Had those friends heeded the Abbot sooner, horse-dragging the corpse, his suffering would have ended—and the later scene of Chongzhen hanging himself on Coal Hill, dying for his country, would never have come.

Cast Off the False Mind, Keep the True Mind

The Avatamsaka Sutra says:

If one wishes to fully understand

All Buddhas of the three periods,

Contemplate the Dharma Realm's nature:

All is made from mind alone.

(If one wishes to understand,

All Buddhas of the three periods,

Contemplate the Dharma Realm's nature:

All is made by mind alone.)

Acting with a Buddha's mind, you are a Buddha; acting with a Bodhisattva's mind, you are a Bodhisattva; acting with a Pratyekabuddha's mind, you are a Pratyekabuddha; acting with a Shravaka's mind, you are a Shravaka; acting with a heaven's mind, you are a heaven; acting with a human's mind, you are a human; acting with an asura's mind, you are an asura; acting with a beast's mind, you are a beast; acting with a hungry ghost's mind, you are a hungry ghost; acting with a hell's mind, you are a hell-ghost.

Hence the saying: "The Ten Dharma Realms never leave a single present thought of mind." Then we know all things are made by mind. A verse on the mind, full of meaning, says:

Three dots like scattered stars;

A curving hook like the crescent moon.

Wearing fur starts from here;

Becoming a Buddha also through it.

A rough translation:

Three dots like a starry host;

A hook curving like the newborn moon.

Growing fur comes from here;

Becoming a Buddha also from here.

Reflect well—the verse is most true.

People in the world must keep the Right Mind, never harboring the deviant mind. What is the Right Mind? The Bodhi mind, the equal mind, the kind mind, the pitying mind, the giving mind, the mind of shame. What is the deviant mind? Selfish minds, self-benefiting, jealous, hateful, arrogant, idle-fancying minds. In cultivation we must aim to cast off the false mind and keep the True Mind—that is, casting off the deviant mind, giving rise to the Right Mind.

If every act of ours holds right mindfulness, that is right knowledge and views; with deviant thoughts come deviant knowledge and views. One with deviant thoughts calls wrong right and right wrong, takes white for black and black for white—upside-down right and wrong, black and white undistinguished. Every act he deems right—yet the fruit is offense; fallen into the hells, still not knowing why. Hence the Buddhas painstakingly exhorted, tirelessly admonishing: "Walk not the wrong road! Enter no dead end!" This also reminds us cultivators never to create evil karma in the Way-place. There is a saying:

Neglect no small good deed; commit no small evil deed.

Hour after hour, minute after minute alert, examining ourselves—trembling as on a deep abyss's edge, as treading thin ice—slowly shedding foul habits, bettering bad conduct, sly tendencies, ghostly cleverness. Examine yourselves in all things clearly—not muddling through the days like the blind leading the blind, deceiving one another, driving the world daily toward crisis—toward the final age, all to destruction.

Those with right mindfulness can lead humankind along the open, upright road. All of one heart, helping one another—you helping me, I helping you—all in mutual aid. There is a saying: "Helping others is the fount of joy," or "doing good is the greatest joy." Resolving on good deeds, the joy no pen describes—only doers of good know its full savor. Try tasting good deeds—how does it feel? That joy is truly wondrous. We must at all costs avoid crooked roads—tripping not only ourselves, but leading others into dead ends. For these reasons, our minds must be upright and bright to shine through and smash all darkness.
